content: In January 1991, an outbreak of epidemic cholera emerged in Peru and rapidly spread to other Latin American countries. The delayed reporting of cholera cases in some regions made it difficult to fully understand the extent of the epidemic. An evaluation of cholera surveillance systems in several countries revealed recurring issues, including challenges with case definitions, laboratory surveillance, surveillance methods, national coordination, and data management. A key finding was that a simple and well-communicated cholera surveillance system during an epidemic is critical for effective prevention and treatment efforts. 1. Simplify case definitions for cholera. 2. Focus laboratory surveillance on patients with diarrhea, especially during the early stages of an epidemic. 3. Use the suspect case definition predominantly when the number of confirmed cases increases. 4. Report weekly data on cases, hospitalizations, and deaths to regional and central levels. 5. Frequently analyze data and distribute weekly or biweekly summaries. 6. Promptly report cholera cases to the World Health Organization (WHO). Background Cholera is a preventable and treatable disease. Prevention and treatment efforts are most effective when there is collaboration between regional, national, and international public health offices. A simple, widely accepted, and well-described surveillance system is the best way to achieve this. When cholera first appeared in Peru in January 1991, it spread rapidly to other Latin American countries. The unexpected nature of the epidemic left some countries unprepared, although many had already developed preparedness plans for cholera control. An ideal cholera control plan includes health education, environmental sanitation, clinical management, laboratory diagnosis, epidemiologic investigation, and surveillance. During the epidemic, epidemiologists from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) identified several recurring problems with cholera surveillance, including difficulties in data collection, transmission, and analysis. These issues often caused delays and obscured the epidemic's scope at regional, national, and international levels. Additionally, some national surveillance systems used complex case definitions, which hindered the rapid and smooth reporting of cases. This report highlights key problems in cholera surveillance systems in Latin America and provides recommendations to improve surveillance at both national and international levels. Case Definitions A major issue in cholera surveillance is the complexity of case definitions. A case definition is a set of objective criteria (symptoms, signs, and laboratory data) used to reliably and consistently identify cases of the disease. Many countries use two main categories for cholera cases: suspect and confirmed. However, within these categories, multiple definitions are often used, which complicates reporting and data analysis. For example: In one country, a suspect case is defined in three ways: (a) profuse diarrhea with severe dehydration in a person of any age, (b) acute diarrhea in an area with confirmed cholera, or (c) acute diarrhea in a person who traveled through an infected area within five days of illness onset. In another country, a suspect case is defined as acute diarrhea in a person aged ≥5 years, with an additional probable case category for dehydrating diarrhea with vomiting, cramps, and malaise in someone epidemiologically linked to other cholera cases. Such multiple definitions increase reporting difficulties and can confuse data analysis. Most countries use 5 years as the lower age limit for cholera surveillance, which aligns with the transition from preschool to school age. This age threshold excludes many non-cholera diarrhea cases, making the definition more specific. The WHO previously recommended 10 years as the lower age limit but is revising this guidance. A confirmed cholera case is typically defined as Vibrio cholerae O1 infection verified by laboratory methods, such as stool culture. In rare cases, additional confirmation of cholera toxin production may be necessary to distinguish toxigenic strains from non-toxigenic ones. Serologic diagnosis, based on antibody titers, is rarely used. However, relying solely on laboratory-confirmed cases can distort the epidemic's true picture, as asymptomatic infections are common during outbreaks. Reporting asymptomatic individuals as confirmed cases can misrepresent surveillance data. The challenge with simple case definitions lies in the wide spectrum of illness caused by cholera. Over 70% of infected individuals are asymptomatic, while 15%-23% experience mild to moderate diarrhea indistinguishable from other causes. Only 2%-5% of infected individuals develop severe dehydrating diarrhea. A case definition based solely on severe diarrhea is more specific but misses many infections. In public health, an accurate count of symptomatic infections is more useful. No single case definition is perfect; a balance between sensitivity and specificity is needed to provide a representative picture of the epidemic. Recommendations: Cholera cases should be categorized as either suspect or confirmed. A suspect case should be defined as acute, watery diarrhea in a person aged ≥5 years. A confirmed case should be defined as laboratory-confirmed Vibrio cholerae O1 infection in any person with diarrhea. Laboratory Confirmation and Environmental Surveillance Laboratories play a central role in cholera surveillance. They confirm the presence of Vibrio cholerae O1 in an area, monitor its persistence, assess its antibiotic susceptibility, and detect its presence in the environment. Preliminary isolation and confirmation require trained personnel using thiosulfate-citrate-bile salts-sucrose (TCBS) agar and polyvalent antisera. During the Latin American cholera epidemic, most countries quickly staffed laboratories with trained personnel and minimal supplies. However, as the epidemic progressed, many laboratories became overwhelmed with the demand for confirming numerous suspect cases, leading to delays in reporting results. Recommendations: Regional laboratories should have trained personnel to confirm Vibrio cholerae O1 using TCBS agar and polyvalent antisera. Central laboratories should confirm field isolates and provide further characterization. In newly affected areas, a sample of suspect cases should be cultured to confirm cholera's presence. Once cholera is established, stool cultures should be limited to monitoring its continued presence and antibiotic susceptibility. In cholera-threatened areas without confirmed cases, Moore swabs can be used to detect Vibrio cholerae O1 in sewage. If detected, laboratory-based surveillance should focus on patients with diarrhea. Stages of Surveillance Cholera surveillance evolves through two stages: 1. Early Stage: Cultures are obtained from many diarrhea patients to diagnose cholera. Only culture-confirmed cases are reported. 2. Later Stage: As cholera becomes widespread, the number of suspect cases more accurately reflects the epidemic's scope. Reporting shifts to include suspect cases to simplify and expedite reporting. Recommendations: In cholera-threatened areas, investigate acute dehydrating diarrhea in persons aged ≥5 years. Shift to using the suspect case definition when confirmed cases increase. Continue reporting suspect cases for at least one year after the epidemic wanes. Communication and Reporting Surveillance data is only valuable if communicated promptly and clearly. Timely reporting of laboratory results allows early identification of affected areas and immediate investigations. Recommendations: Treatment centers and regional offices should report surveillance data weekly to a central office using rapid methods (e.g., radio, telephone). Surveillance data should be analyzed promptly and disseminated to all levels. International Reporting Cholera is one of three internationally notifiable diseases. Countries are required to report cases to WHO promptly. While some governments may fear economic consequences (e.g., reduced tourism or food exports), accurate reporting improves resource allocation and control efforts. Recommendations: Countries should report cholera cases to WHO in a timely and accurate manner.
